equivalent: `flo` reaches the loop body only through `opposite(flo, .)`, and `opposite` reads its first argument through exactly two predicates, `a <= 0.0` and `a >= 0.0`. On any value with a sign those two resolve the whole test: for a > 0 it is `b <= 0.0`, for a < 0 it is `b >= 0.0`, and for a == 0 (either zero) it is `true` whatever `b` is. So `opposite` is a function of the SIGN CLASS of its first argument and nothing else. The loop now refuses a NaN midpoint before the test (`if fmid.is_nan() { return None; }`), so `flo` always has a sign class -- an infinity has one too, which is why only NaN is refused. The branch that moves `lo` is `!opposite(flo, fmid)`, which for flo > 0 forces fmid > 0 and for flo < 0 forces fmid < 0, and which is unreachable for flo == 0; the carried `fmid` therefore always lands in the same sign class as the stale `flo`, and every later `opposite` resolves identically whichever of the two is held. The two programs take the same branch on every iteration and return the same f64. The assignment is kept because it makes the invariant local rather than something a reader has to reconstruct. (Before the `is_nan` guard this argument was FALSE: a NaN f(mid) took the lo-moving branch, was carried into `flo`, and made every later `opposite` false, so the unmutated loop answered Some(-40.0) -- the bracket endpoint -- where the mutant answered -65.0, the root. MEASURED on `bisect_rest(|v| if v == -65.0 { f64::NAN } else { v + 65.0 })`.)
